newsitem.title: THAILAND: Changes loom as Thai brokers face mounting woes.
newsitem.headline: Changes loom as Thai brokers face mounting woes.

text.p: Tough times and major changes lie ahead for Thai finance and securities companies struggling to cope with rising costs and deteriorating asset quality, industry executives and analysts said.
Declining confidence in Thailand's slowing economy, high current account deficit and plunging stock market has raised concerns over the financial stability of large and small finance firms.
To survive, some of the smaller firms might have to merge, analysts said.

Thai stocks, plummeting to more than 4-1/2 lows under the weight of weak economic fundamentals, have reduced the asset quality of finance firms, increased their funding costs and sharply trimmed the sector's earnings this year, analysts said.

"It is very hard to see how these companies make money in this environment...we expect sector earnings could fall by as much as 60 percent this year," Ian Gisbourne, finance and securities analyst at SBC Warburg, told Reuters.

A central bank policy of keeping high short-term interest rates to discourage speculation against the baht has produced a severe cash crunch for finance companies that normally raise about 30 percent of their funds in the overnight market.
"There are liquidity problems in the sector, and cash flow for many companies is quite tight right now," said Suchat Boonbanjerdsri, managing director of Dynamic Eastern Finance and Securities.
"I think there are some companies, though it is not possible to say how many, which are having difficulties issuing bills of exchange and promissory notes," Suchat said.
Though the central bank has said it will help finance firms tie over cash flow shortages, analysts fear their longer-term outlook remains unstable.
"Companies are paying too much for their funds which they are then lent to people who are not paying the interest. This situation is simply not sustainable," Gisbourne said.
The finance sector has been hurt by a prolonged slump in the local property market that has eroded the quality of its assets, analysts said.
Thailand's 91 finance and securities companies, of which 51 are listed, have made an average 25 percent of their combined 1.5 trillion baht ($58 billion) loans to the property sector.
Combined with falling equity broking revenue and portfolio losses from bearish stocks, the declining outlook spells imminent changes for the finance industry, executives and analysts said.
"I don't think it will come in the form of mergers and acquisitions, but I think in friendly and constructive consolidation," Suchat said.

About 48 Thai finance and securities firms have parent banks or strong foreign links to help them weather the market downturn, but analysts said the sooner that smaller, independent operators join forces, the healthier their prospects for survival.
"Consolidation in whatever form is a concept that should be welcomed in the sector. Egos should not get in the way. Every one should accept it and be humble," Suchat said.
